snip.t: *Herpes zoster scars:* Multi-dermatomal scarring indicating prior severe varicella-zoster reactivation.
*Stage 2:* Mild symptoms; unexplained moderate weight loss, recurrent respiratory infections, herpes zoster, angular cheilitis, fungal nail infections.
Infection risk: immunosuppression + disease activity ↑ bacterial, viral (especially TB, herpes zoster) and opportunistic infections.
○ Viral infection (e.g., human parvovirus, hepatitis C, hepatitis B, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV),\ncytomegalovirus, herpes zoster varicella, HIV)

After primary infection, varicella-zoster virus becomes latent in spinal and cranial nerve roots and ganglia, and reactivation occurs as herpes zoster that can be accompanied by mild meningoencephalitis.
Tenderness — trauma, costochondritis, rib metastases, herpes zoster (before rash appears), intercostal muscle pain

qs.q: Following primary infection with varicella-zoster virus, where does the virus become latent, leading to potential reactivation as herpes zoster?
o: Spinal and cranial nerve roots and ganglia
Microglial cells residing in basal structures
Glial cells located within the cerebral cortex
Endothelial cells lining brain capillary walls
qs.e: Varicella-zoster virus becomes latent in spinal and cranial nerve roots and ganglia after primary infection. Reactivation can manifest as herpes zoster accompanied by mild meningoencephalitis.
